title: FairBatch: heuristic hypersearch notebook for fairness-aware continuous batching
content:
Context and goal:
This notebook collects experiments and notes for a heuristic hyper-parameter search aimed at finding scheduler configurations that trade off throughput vs. tail latency while enforcing a quantitative fairness constraint across client priority classes. The existing continuous-batching scheduler shows good mean latency but uneven P95/P99 for lower-priority traffic during microburst load. We want a practical config discovery workflow (not an exhaustive grid) that surfaces robust candidates for canary rollout.

Motivation and constraints:
- Product SLA: soft P95 < 120ms, hard P99 < 350ms for default tier; lower tiers allowed higher P99 but must not be starved.
- Deployment: must work with current runtime preemption primitives and prefix KV cache behavior. No kernel changes.
- Search budget: target ~200 evaluation points per experiment run (to keep CI time reasonable).

Hypothesis:
- A fairness penalty term in batch scoring (penalize over-served classes) combined with adaptive timeout scaling per-priority will reduce P99 tail for low-priority traffic with <7% throughput loss for high-priority traces.
- Small batch-padding (microbatching up to 4) reduces variance caused by uneven arrival without hurting latency much for short-context requests.

Experiment harness (synthgen-v2):
- Synth load generator supports: poisson, bursty (on/off), bimodal size distribution, correlated arrivals (session-level bursts).
- Key params we sweep: arrival_pattern, mean_qps, burst_pct, priority_mix, seq_len_dist, kv_cache_hit_rate, deadline_slo_ms.
- Example run: synthgen-v2 --pattern bursty --qps 600 --burst-pct 0.35 --mix 0.6:0.3:0.1 --seq-dist short:0.7,long:0.3 --kv-hit 0.65 --duration 20m

Scheduler knobs (tunable):
- max_batch_tokens: {512, 1024, 2048}
- soft_timeout_ms: {6, 12, 20, 40} (applied per-window, then scaled by priority multiplier)
- priority_time_multiplier: {0.6, 1, 1.6} (low < 1 to favor high priority)
- fairness_penalty_alpha: {0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5} (penalty weight in batch_score)
- pad_to_multiple_of: {1, 8, 16, 32} (microbatch padding)
- allow_preemption: {true, false}

Fairness penalty formula (implementation detail):
- batch_score = base_score - alpha * max(0, served_ratio[class] - target_ratio[class])
- served_ratio = rolling count of tokens served per class normalized by time window
- target_ratio derived from priority_mix (but constrained to min_share per class)
Notes: alpha tuned to penalize aggressive domination but avoid oscillation. Smoothing window = 30s by default.

Profiling instrumentation used:
- tracer: per-request timestamps at enqueue, dequeue, kernel-start, kernel-end, encode/deserialize, kv-cache-lookup; these are exported as CSV for analysis.
- GPU counters: peak SM utilization, average occupancy, memory bandwidth (nvprof/cupti hooks for offline runs).
- Runtime logs: batch composition snapshots every 10s (counts per priority, token totals, pad overhead).

Representative experiment: fairness-alpha sweep under moderate bursty load
- Synthesis: bursty pattern, mean_qps=700, priority_mix=0.5:0.3:0.2, seq_len: short=0.8,long=0.2, kv_hit=0.75
- Fixed knobs: max_batch_tokens=1024, pad_to_multiple_of=8, allow_preemption=true, priority_time_multiplier=1
- Sweep fairness_penalty_alpha in {0.0,0.1,0.25,0.5}

Results summary (aggregated):
- alpha=0.0 (baseline): overall throughput 100% baseline, high-priority P99=90ms, mid-priority P99=180ms, low-priority P99=610ms (severe tail).
- alpha=0.1: throughput -3.2%; high-priority P99=98ms, mid-prio P99=140ms, low-prio P99=260ms (dramatic improvement).
- alpha=0.25: throughput -6.8%; high-prio P99=120ms, mid-prio P99=160ms, low-prio P99=220ms. Some impact to high-priority mean latency observed.
- alpha=0.5: throughput -12.5%; high-prio P99=170ms, mid-prio P99=200ms, low-prio P99=210ms. Overshoots fairness, harming overall SLA.

Interpretation:
- Small alpha (0.1) gives the best practical trade-off: protects low-priority tail without violating high-priority SLA by much. Alpha beyond ~0.25 starts costing too much throughput/latency for high-priority.
- The smoothing window (30s) prevented overreactive throttling in the presence of burst edges. Reducing the window to 5s caused oscillation (observed as feed-back loop with preemption).

Microbatching and pad engineering results:
- pad_to_multiple_of=8 reduces padding overhead for short sequences while enabling denser GPU kernels. Measured token fill factor increased from 62% -> 81% on typical traces.
- However, larger pad alignment (32) increased P99 for short requests due to extra model work (padding) if batch formation waited too long. So prefer 8 or 16 for our workloads.

KV cache interaction notes:
- Lower cache hit rates (<=40%) exacerbate variance: more long sequences (cache-miss) dominate batch token count and push P99 up. The scheduler must detect token-skew and prefer forming mixed batches (long+short) vs. long-only to amortize kernel cost.
- Implemented a simple token-skew detector: if >60% tokens in pending window are long, temporarily cap max_batch_tokens to avoid unbounded growth in latency. This reduced long-only P99 by ~18%.

Profiling excerpt (example lines from batch snapshot CSV):
- ts,window_id,total_batches,total_tokens,avg_batch_fill,pct_pad,high_count,mid_count,low_count
- 1700000,178,320,742,0.78,0.12,112,88,78
- 1700010,179,204,680,0.84,0.06,100,54,50

GPU counter summary for alpha=0.1 run:
- avg SM util: 62% (down from 68% baseline due to smaller batch formation at burst edges)
- mem bw: 210 GB/s avg, peak 246 GB/s
- kernel time variance: reduced for mixed batches vs long-only batches.

Failure modes observed / gotchas:
- Preemption + small smoothing window caused priority inversion spikes (we saw <1% of requests artificially preempted multiple times). Mitigation: add backoff to preemption (cooldown 300ms per preempted request).
- Race between KV-cache eviction and batch formation: evicted keys caused cache-miss waves that looked like a synthetic burst. Solution: add simple eviction jittering + awareness in synthgen to reproduce.

Actionable recommendations (for canary):
1) Candidate config A (conservative): alpha=0.1, max_batch_tokens=1024, pad=8, soft_timeout=12ms, priority_time_multiplier=1.0, smoothing=30s, allow_preemption=true, preempt_cooldown=300ms. Rationale: best balance of fairness and high-priority SLA preservation.
2) Candidate config B (aggressive fairness): alpha=0.25, max_batch_tokens=1024, pad=8, soft_timeout=12ms, priority_time_multiplier=1.0, smoothing=30s, allow_preemption=true. Use only for limited traffic % (5-10%) during staged rollout.
3) Avoid alpha >= 0.5 in production — overheads and throughput loss observed.

Planned follow-ups and experiments:
- Run same heuristic search but with dynamic priority multipliers (learn a small online multiplier per-class using low-frequency PID controller) to see if we can close gap between A and B without throughput loss.
- More thorough KV-cache stress tests: orchestrate controlled eviction events and measure cold-start P99 across classes.
- Explore lightweight ML-guided scoring: small XGBoost model that predicts batch score using recent window features; compare to simple alpha penalty baseline.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- What is acceptable throughput regression (percent) for a fairness improvement? Ops/PM input required.
- Should mid-tier customers get independent min_share config, or do we keep single global target_ratio mapping?

Notes to reviewers:
- The notebook includes raw CSVs and the harness script used (github PR linked above). If you want to reproduce, run the synth command with --seed and the attached config.
- Slack thread: #serving-batching contains some anecdotal customer reports that motivated this work; see message ids in linked artifacts.

Appendix: quick commands
- Run a single evaluation: ./harness/run_eval.sh --config configs/fairbatch/alpha-0.1.yaml --duration 20m --out out/alpha-0.1
- Aggregate results: python tools/aggregate_results.py out/* --metrics p95 p99 throughput pad_overhead
- Generate plots: python tools/plot_batch_metrics.py out/alpha-*.csv --save figs/fairbatch_alpha_sweep.png

End of notebook.

(Marcus C., Leah I., Diego R. — please add raw CSVs and any extra profiling snippets you want archived here.)
